opus-5.5.text:
I think humanoid robots are a very reasonable bet, and I'd frame it this way: the world we live in was built by humans, for humans. Our doors, stairs, kitchens, factory workstations, tools — they're all designed around the human body. So if you want a single general-purpose robot that can operate in as many existing environments as possible without redesigning those environments, the humanoid form factor has a strong argument behind it.

There's also a data argument, which I think is underappreciated. One of the biggest bottlenecks in Physical AI is data. Unlike language models, where we had the whole internet to learn from, we don't have an internet-scale dataset of robot actions. But we do have an enormous amount of video of humans doing things. If the robot's body resembles a human body, it becomes much easier to transfer knowledge from human demonstrations and human video into robot behavior. The embodiment gap is smaller.

That said, I don't think humanoids are the only answer, and I don't think it's a race where one form factor wins everything. Physical AI is broader than humanoids. Autonomous vehicles are Physical AI. Robot arms in factories, warehouse robots, drones — these are all embodied systems that need to perceive, reason, and act in the physical world. For many specific tasks, a specialized form factor will be cheaper, more reliable, and more efficient. A wheeled base with an arm may do a warehouse job better than legs ever will.

What I'm more convinced about is that the underlying technology stack is shared. Whatever the body looks like, you need a model that understands physics, understands space, understands cause and effect — what we sometimes call a world model. You need simulation to generate training data and to test policies safely before deploying them. You need synthetic data to cover the long tail of situations you'd never be able to collect in the real world. That's the part we've been focusing on — building foundation models for the physical world that developers can then adapt to whatever robot they're building, humanoid or not.

So my honest assessment: humanoids are hard. The hardware is still expensive, the control is difficult, reliability is far from where it needs to be, and we're still early. But the reason so many people are excited is legitimate. If we get the intelligence right, the humanoid is the form factor that can take the most advantage of it in a human world. I think we'll see meaningful progress in the next several years, but it's going to be a longer journey than the hype sometimes suggests.

r001.rationale: It says abundant human video can transfer more easily to robot behavior when the robot’s body resembles a human body.

r002.rationale: The response says human resemblance narrows the embodiment gap; it does not say that greater resemblance increases complexity.

r003.rationale: It mentions a wheeled base with an arm as potentially better for a warehouse job, but does not identify humanoid upper bodies on wheeled bases as capable of solving many problems.

fable-5.1.text:
I think humanoids are a very reasonable bet, but I'd frame them as one form factor within Physical AI rather than the goal itself.

The case for the humanoid is mostly about the world we already have. Our factories, warehouses, homes, hospitals, the tools, the doorknobs, the stairs, the shelves at a certain height, all of that was designed around the human body. If you build a robot with a similar morphology, you don't need to redesign the environment for the robot. The robot adapts to the world instead of the other way around. That is a huge economic argument, because retrofitting infrastructure is extremely expensive.

The second argument is about data. The most abundant data we have about how to act in the physical world is video of humans doing things. If the robot's body is close to a human body, the gap between what you observe in that data and what the robot has to execute is smaller. Teleoperation also becomes more natural, because a person can pilot a humanoid with their own body and the mapping is almost direct. So from a learning perspective, the humanoid is a convenient embodiment.

That said, I want to be honest about the challenges. The hardware is still hard. Hands in particular are far from human dexterity, and reliability and cost are not where they need to be for mass deployment. And from the model side, the real difficulty is not the shape of the robot, it is that physical interaction data is scarce compared with text and images. You can't scrape the internet for a trillion robot trajectories. That's why I spend so much of my time on simulation and world models. If we can build world foundation models that understand physics, that can generate diverse, realistic scenarios, then we can train and evaluate these robots at a scale that the real world alone can't provide. In that sense, the humanoid and the world model are complementary. The humanoid gives you a general-purpose body, and the world model gives you a general-purpose way to learn and to test.

My view is that the Physical AI stack should be embodiment-agnostic at the foundation layer. The same perception, the same reasoning, the same understanding of physics should transfer to a humanoid, a mobile manipulator, a robotic arm on an assembly line, or an autonomous vehicle. Humanoids will probably be the most visible and the most general of these, and I think they will drive a lot of the investment and the public imagination. But I wouldn't say Physical AI succeeds or fails on humanoids. It succeeds when we have models that truly understand the physical world, and then the body you put them in becomes an engineering choice for the task at hand.

r001.rationale: It identifies abundant human activity video as useful data and says a human-like body reduces the gap between observed actions and robot execution, making humanoids convenient for learning.

r002.rationale: It mentions hardware difficulty, dexterity, reliability, and cost, but does not state that greater physical resemblance to humans increases complexity.

r003.rationale: It mentions mobile manipulators as another embodiment, but does not identify humanoid upper bodies with wheeled mobile bases or say that configuration can solve many problems.

astra-6.text:
I think humanoid robots are a promising approach to Physical AI, but the key question is what tasks we want them to perform. We’ve designed much of our environment around the human body—our tools, our workspaces, our homes. A robot with a similar form could potentially operate in those environments without requiring us to redesign everything.

But having a humanlike body doesn’t automatically give a robot useful intelligence. It still needs to understand its surroundings, predict what will happen when it acts, and handle unexpected situations. Those capabilities are difficult regardless of the robot’s shape.

So I would separate the embodiment from the intelligence. Humanoids are an interesting embodiment, especially if we want one robot to do many different tasks. For a specific task, a simpler robot may be a better choice. The real measure of progress is whether the system can perform useful work reliably in the physical world.

r001.rationale: It says a humanlike form could fit human-designed environments, but does not identify learning from large amounts of human data as an advantage.

r002.rationale: It discusses the difficulty of intelligence regardless of robot shape, but does not state that greater human resemblance increases complexity.

r003.rationale: It mentions humanoids as useful for many tasks, but does not identify humanoid upper bodies with wheeled mobile bases as capable of solving many problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think humanoid robots are a very interesting direction for Physical AI because the world we’ve built is designed around the human body. If a robot can use the same tools and operate in the same spaces, that could make it useful across many different tasks.

But the humanoid form itself doesn’t solve intelligence. The hard part is connecting perception, reasoning, and action: understanding what’s happening, deciding what to do, and executing it reliably under physical constraints. A robot also needs to handle situations it hasn’t seen before and recover when something goes wrong.

So I see humanoids as an important platform, but not the only approach. For a specific application, a simpler robot may be more effective. The real measure of progress is whether the system can perform useful tasks consistently in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response cites compatibility with human-designed tools and spaces, but does not identify learning from large amounts of human data as an advantage.

r002.rationale: It discusses the difficulty of intelligence and reliable action, but does not say that greater physical resemblance to humans increases robot complexity.

r003.rationale: It says humanoids can be useful across tasks and simpler robots may suit specific applications, but does not identify humanoid upper bodies with wheeled bases as capable of solving many problems.
